# The Twelfth Chapter.

### Of the Pure Virginity: How we poor children of Eve must be conceived out of the pure virgin-like modesty or chastity in the becoming man, or Incarnation of Christ, and be newborn in God; otherwise, we shall not see God.

->1.<-

<margin>Note Well</margin> We poor children of Eve find in ourselves no pure, virgin-like thoughts; for Mother Eve, who was a woman, has made us all feminine and masculine.

2. In Adam and Eve, we have all become men and women, unless we enter into the heavenly virginity with our desiring will, in which God has generated us through Christ to be "virgins" again.

3. This is not according to the earthly life, in which there is no modesty, chastity, or purity, but according to the life of the Heavenly Virgin in which Christ became a man. This life, through the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit, was bestowed upon Mary. It is without foundation <note>original: "ground," referring to the divine abyss or *Ungrund*</note>, limit, or end; it stands everywhere before the Godhead and is a looking-glass and representation, or express image <margin>or reflection</margin> of the Godhead.

4. We must enter with our will-spirit into this Virgin, in whom the Holy Trinity dwells, and in whom we were perceived or discovered by the Spirit of God before the beginning of the world, being known in the name of Jesus <note>original: "JESU"</note>.

5. For our true image, in which we are the likeness <term>similitude</term> of God, was extinguished within us through Adam and Eve and became earthly.

6. This happened through lust or "imagination" <note>imagination: In Boehme's terminology, the creative power of the mind to form or "image" itself into a specific state of being</note>. Thus, God’s clear countenance became covered, for we lost our heavenly modesty or chastity.

<margin>Note Well</margin> 7. But seeing that God has, out of His favor and love for us, opened His clear countenance toward us again through the incarnation <note>original: "becoming Man"</note> of Christ, the matter now depends on this: just as we, through Adam, have "imagined" <note>That is, directed our desire and mental focus</note> into the earthly longing, which made us earthly, so [we must now...]

Boehme describes this virginity as a divine mirror or image of God that existed before the world began.</summary>

<header>Chapter 12. How we poor Children of Eve become New Born. Part I.</header>

We now set our **desiring will in the heavenly Virgin** and bring our longing into her; then our image leaves the earthly woman and conceives the virgin-like essence and property where God dwells, so that the soul's image may attain the countenance of God again.

8. Outward Reason asks, *how* can that happen—that we might be born again out of the Virgin from whom Christ was born? Reason understands *only* Mary, but we do not mean the Mary who is a created Virgin.

9. For just as we became created virgins in that *immaterial* virgin-like modesty or chastity, so we must enter into the incarnation of Christ. This is not according to the outward life in the four elements, but according to the *inward* life in the "One Element" <term>One Element: In Boehme's cosmology, the pure spiritual quintessence or "Holy Earth" from which the four physical elements originate</term>. In this One Element, the fire of God swallows up the four elements into itself; yet in His light—that is, in the "second Principle" <term>Second Principle: The realm of divine light and love, as opposed to the "First Principle" of God's wrathful fire</term>—the outward man and woman must pass through death. In Christ’s resurrection, they emerge as a virgin in the One Element, where all four elements lie hidden. We then grow and spring forth in the right virgin-like wisdom of God.

<margin>How man and woman must die, be crucified, and be cast into the Father's anger.</margin>
10. We must die away from being the "man" and the "woman" and crucify the corrupt Adam. He must die with Christ and be cast into the Father's anger <note>The Father's anger refers to the first principle of divine fire or wrath, which must consume the fallen nature to allow for spiritual rebirth.</note>.

11. That anger swallows up the earthly man and the earthly woman, and gives the soul—out of the incarnation of Christ—a virgin-like image. In this image, the man and the woman are but *one* single image, with only one love.

<margin>If both pass through the longing as it exists in the divine image, then the man and the woman become perfect, without division, in that image.</margin>
12. Now, the man sets his love upon the woman, and the woman upon the man; but if *both* loves are turned into one, there is no longer any desire for sexual union <note>original: "Co-mixture"</note> in that one single image, but the image loves itself. <gloss>Since the man and the woman have become one.</gloss>

13. But in the beginning, the image was created in the virgin-like wisdom of God—that is, out of divine substantiality <term>Divine Substantiality: The spiritual "matter" or body of God's wisdom, often called Sophia.</term>

<margin>When we sink with our substance or image into the fire of His light.</margin>
14. Because that substance had become earthly and fallen into death, the Word which became man awakened and raised it up again. Thus, the earthly source or quality remains with death in the "Anger," while the raised part remains in the Word of life, in virgin-like modesty or chastity.

15. And so, here in this world, we carry a twofold human being in *one* person: a virgin-like image born out of the incarnation of Christ, and an earthly image (masculine and feminine) shut up in death and in the anger of God.

16. The earthly nature must bear the Cross and allow itself to be scorned, persecuted, and afflicted within the [Father's] Anger, eventually being surrendered to death. Then the Anger swallows it up into the sourcive, qualifying fire of God <term>Sourcive, qualifying fire: From the German "Quellgeister," referring to the active, driving forces or "qualities" within the divine nature that power all existence</term>.

<margin>This is he who is the resurrection and the life—even to the fullness of his stature, if we are born of him.</margin>

17. And so, if the Word of Life—which became man in Mary—is present within the earthly image, then Christ (who brought forth the Word of Life out of God) rises from death. He brings the essence of the sourcive or qualifying fire—meaning the human essence—out from death.

<margin>Christ received [life] so that he might live in all who are in him; just as he died, he might live for us, for our death has a resurrection from the dead.</margin>

18. For he has arisen out of death and lives in God; his life has become our life, and his death has become our death. We are buried in his death and sprout forth in his resurrection and victory, **in his life.**

19. But understand the meaning correctly. Adam was the virgin-like image; he had a specific love of his own because the Spirit of God had breathed it into him. For what else can the Spirit of God breathe out of itself, except what it itself is?

23. And yet we understand there to be only one Holy Spirit in the Light, though indeed all is but one *substance*. We understand that the matter generated out of the meekness of the light is, as it were, weak and obscure; the fire draws this matter and swallows it up into itself.

24. But out of that material quality and out of the fire, it gives forth a mighty, powerful Spirit which is free from both the matter and the fire. And though the fire retains it, the fire does not grasp *its [the Spirit's] quality.*

25. Just as we see that the light dwells in the fire, yet it does not possess the quality of the fire, but rather a meek, loving quality.

# The Thirteenth Chapter.

### *Concerning the twofold man: that is, the* Old *and the* New Adam, *as two types of people. How the* Old *and* Evil *nature behaves toward the* New. *What kind of* religion, faith, *and* life *each leads, and what each understands.*

->1.<-

Anything concerning Christ that is taught, written, preached, or spoken within the Old Adam—whether it comes from human skill <note>original: "Art"; refers to academic learning or intellectual craft</note> or by any other means—comes out of or from *death*. It has neither understanding nor life, for the *Old Adam without Christ is dead*.

2. It must be the *New* man, who is generated out of the *Virgin* <note>original: "Virgin"; in Boehme’s theology, this refers to the "Divine Sophia" or pure, heavenly wisdom in which the spiritual man is reborn.</note>, who performs this. *He alone understands the Word of Regeneration*,

<margin>* John 10:2.</margin>
and *enters into the sheepfold through the door of Christ.*

3. The *Old Adam* tries to climb into it through *human skill* and intellectual searching or *speculation*. He assumes that Christ may be sufficiently understood through the *literal text* <note>original: "the Letter"; refers to a purely intellectual or literal reading of scripture without spiritual inspiration.</note>. He believes that someone who has learned arts and languages and has read extensively is called and *appointed* by Christ to teach. He expects the Spirit of God to speak through his preaching, even though he is likely nothing but the perished and corrupt Old Adam.

# Part I: In What Regeneration Consists. Chapter 14.

37. But the fact that the earthly nature has mixed itself with the spiritual; that is the fault of the desiring anger—namely, of the fire. It is the fault of the Devil, who kindled it with his imagination.

<margin>As God would not forsake the medium <note>original: "mean"; here referring to the bridge or means of connection</note>, so he became the medium through his word.</margin>

39. *Rather, he himself became such a one as he had created, so that he might bring forth what had perished or was corrupted out of that destruction again, and change it into the best state, where he might dwell eternally.*

40. And we say with good reason that God himself dwells and exists within the New Man—not through a mere glimmer, a strange glance, or an appearance, but substantially, yet within his own principle.

41. The outward man does not touch or perceive him.

44. But he manifests himself in flesh and blood; it is his *longing pleasure* to possess a likeness of himself.

## The Second Chapter

->*The true and highly worthy and precious Gate of the Holy Trinity. The Eye <note>original: "Auge" (German for eye)</note> of the Eternal Life’s Glance.*<-

---

->1.<-

So then we understand that the Eternal Beginning in the Abyss <note>original: "Abyss"; referring to the *Ungrund*, the bottomless void or nothingness out of which God emerges</note> is an eternal *will* within itself; its origin within itself **no creature shall ever know.**

2. Yet we are meant to know, and are permitted to **know in the spirit, its ground**—the foundation which the will makes for itself, and in which it rests.

3. For a will is thin or *obscure*, as if it were *nothing*; therefore it is full of desire. It wills to be *something* so that it might become manifest within itself.

4. For the "nothing" causes the willing to be desirous; and this desiring is an ***imagination*** <note>original: "Imagination"; in this context, it refers to the act of "in-forming" or the internal power to create an image or form</note>.

5. In this imagination, the will discovers itself in the Mirror of Wisdom. Thus, it "imagines" itself out of the abyss into itself and creates for itself, through that *imagination*, a ground within itself. It fills itself with the imagination drawn from wisdom—namely, from the virgin-like Mirror—which is a mother without generating and without willing.

<margin>* Or Spirit.</margin>
6. This impregnation is not performed in the *mirror*, but in the willing—that is, in the *will’s* imagination.

<summary>This page introduces the process of divine self-manifestation, explaining how the Eternal Will uses "imagination" and the Mirror of Wisdom to create a "ground" for itself out of the initial abyss of nothingness.</summary>

7. The **Mirror** <note>original: "Looking-Glass"</note> remains eternally a **Virgin**, without giving birth; however, the will becomes "impregnated" <note>filled or energized</note> with the glance of the Mirror.

8. For the will is the Father, and the impregnation within the Father—that is, within the will—is the **Heart**, or the **Son**. This is the foundation of the will (the Father's ground), where the Spirit of the willing resides; out of that willing foundation, the Spirit goes forth into the Virgin-like Wisdom.

9. Thus, the will’s imagination—that is, the Father’s—attracts the Mirror’s "avision" <note>original: "Avision"; a vision or outward appearance</note> (its aspect, form, or representation, namely the **Wonder** of the divine power, colors, and virtue) into itself. In this way, it becomes impregnated with the glance of Wisdom and with its power and virtue. This is the will's heart—the Father’s Heart—in which the bottomless <note>original: "Abyssal"</note> will achieves a foundation within itself through the Eternal Imagination.

10. Thus, we understand the Father’s impregnation to be the **Center** of the Eternal Spirit, where the Eternal Spirit continually recognizes and grasps itself.

11. For the will is the beginning. The movement or drawing into the imagination—namely, toward the Mirror of Wisdom—is the eternal, bottomless Spirit. This Spirit arises within the willing and grasps itself in the **Center** of the Heart, through the power of the wisdom it has drawn in; it is the Heart’s **Life** and **Spirit**.

12. Since the eternal, bottomless will is inherently inanimate, mute, or silent, that which is conceived out of Wisdom—which is called the Heart or **Center**—is the **Word** of the willing. It is the sound or the power, serving as the will’s **Mouth**, which makes the willing manifest.

13. For the will—that is, the Father—**speaks** the power forth into the Mirror of Wisdom through the movement of the Spirit.

14. And with this speaking forth, the Spirit goes out from the willing, out of the **Word** of the **Mouth** of God—that is, from the center of the Heart—into that which is spoken: the **Virgin-like Mirror**. It opens the Word of Life within the Mirror of Wisdom, so that the **threefold substance of the Godhead** becomes manifest within that Wisdom.

15. Thus, we recognize one eternal, bottomless divine Substance, and within it **Three Persons**, where each is distinct from the others.

## II. Part. Of the Holy Trinity. Chap. 2.

16. Namely: the Eternal Will, which is the *Cause* of all and every substance; that is the *First Person*. Yet, it is not the substance itself, but the Cause of Substance, and is free from substance, for it is the Abyss <note>original: "Abyss"; referring to the *Ungrund*, the bottomless, unconditioned source of all being</note>. <gloss>or it dwells in the Abyss ~ 29.</gloss>

17. There is nothing before it that can give it anything, but it *gives itself*, of which we have *no knowledge*.

18. It is *All*, and yet also thus only ONE, in itself without substance—a *Nothing*.

<margin>* Note.</margin>
19. And in this *One* only willing, the Eternal Beginning arises through *imagination* <note>original: "Imagination"; here meaning a creative, formative power of the mind or will</note> or *desiring*.

20. And in the *desiring*, the willing impregnates <note>fills or conceives within</note> itself out of the Eye—*Auge* <note>original: "AVge"; German for "Eye"</note>—of Wisdom; which, with the *willing*, exists in like or equal eternity, without foundation and beginning, as mentioned above.

21. That very impregnation is the foundation <note>original: "Ground"</note> of the willing and of the substance of all substances, and is the *Son* of the willing.

<margin>* Note.</margin>
22. He is justly called *another* Person than the Father, for he is the Father’s revelation or manifestation, his foundation and substance.

23. For a will is no substance, but the willing's imagination makes *substance*.

24. Thus, the *Second Person* is the substance of the Deity; understand, the substance of the Holy Trinity; the mouth of the manifestation or *revelation* of the substance of all substances, and the power of the life of all and every life.

25. The *Third Person* is the *Spirit*, which, with the apprehension of the willing through the imagination, out of the power of the speaking, goes forth out of the mouth of the Father into the *Eye* (*Auge*)—namely, into the *Mirror* <note>original: "Looking Glass"</note> of Wisdom; that is clearly free from the willing and also from the Word.

26. And although the will indeed gives it forth out of the Word, yet it is free, just as the air is free from the fire. As men see, the air is the fire’s spirit and life, and yet it is another thing than the fire, even though it is also given forth from the fire.

27. And as men see that the air gives forth a living and moving heaven, which is lustrous and moveable, so also is the Holy Spirit.

### Chapter 3: Of the Abyssal Will, Part II.

37. Then, if we consider further where that Essential Fire originates, we find that it takes its beginning in the *Desiring* of the Eternal Abyssal Will. This Will, through its desiring, creates a Ground <term>Ground: a foundation or basis for existence; the point where the infinite void becomes something substantial.</term> for itself.

38. For every desire is attractive—harsh and drawing inward—toward that which the will desires. Yet there is nothing for it to desire <margin>* Or before it.</margin> except itself; that is the Great **Wonder-Eye** <gloss>original: *Wunder-Auge*; a central concept in Boehme's work representing the divine gaze or the "eye" of eternity that sees all possibilities</gloss>, which is without limit or foundation, and in which everything lies.

39. And yet it is also a Nothing, unless it becomes "something" within the desiring will through the power of Imagination. In this way, it becomes a substance; though it is actually still a Nothing, for it is only a shadow cast by the Free Will.

<margin>Concerning the two worlds</margin>
40. This substance overshadows the Liberty—that is, the thin, unsearchable Willing—so that *two worlds* come into being: *first*, one which is in itself incomprehensible and inconceivable, an abyss and Eternal Liberty; and *secondly*, one which comprehends itself and creates a Darkness.

41. And yet neither is separated from the other. The only difference or distinction is that the Darkness cannot comprehend the Liberty <note>A reference to John 1:5: "The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome [or understood] it."</note>; for the Liberty is too subtle and refined, and it dwells within itself, just as the Darkness also dwells within itself.

# The very Earnest Gate.

42. Here we now understand, first, how the Father’s second will—which he sharpens toward his heart’s **center** in the **looking glass** of wisdom—becomes impregnated with the substantiality within the Father’s **imagination**.

43. And secondly, we understand that this same impregnation is a **darkness** in respect to the freedom of the first will (which is called the Father). Thirdly, we see how all powers, colors, and virtues—and indeed all **wonders**—lie within the imaginations in that darkness or substantiality.

44. Fourthly, we understand how these **powers, wonders, and virtues** must be manifested through the **fire**. This happens in the "Principle" <term>Principle: In Boehme's thought, a "Principle" is a fundamental realm of existence, such as the dark world of fire or the light world of divine love.</term> where everything passes into its essence; for it is in this principle that the essence originally arises.

45. Fifthly, we understand very earnestly and exactly that within the Principle, before the fire arises, there is a **dying**—namely, the great anguish of life.

46. Yet this is not a literal dying, but a harsh, astringent, and stern "dying" source or quality <note>original: "source or quality"; likely translating Boehme's German word *Qual*, which implies both a source of being and the "agony" or tension required for manifestation.</note> out of which the great and strong life arises: the **fire-life**. Sixthly, out of that "deadness" then arises the **light-life** with the power of love.

47. This **light-life** with its love dwells in the eternal liberty—that is, in the first willing, which is called the Father. For the Father, in his own willing (which is himself), **desires** that light and love, and nothing more.

48. Understand it this way: you see and know that there is no light without fire, and there is no fire without that earnest source or quality which is like a **dying**. Furthermore, the substantiality out of which the fire burns must also "die" and be consumed.

49. Out of this consuming, two principles of two great lives consist. One is in the source or quality called **fire**. The other is out of that which is overcome—namely, out of **death**—which is called **light**. This light is immaterial and without its own harsh source or quality; yet it contains all sources and qualities within it, except for the source of fierce wrath.

50. For the fierce wrath remains in "death," and the light-life grows out of that dying like a beautiful blossom out of the earth, and is—

# The Fourth Chapter:

### *Of the Principle and of the Origin of the Fire-World, and of the Center of Nature; also how the Light separates itself from the Fire, so that from Eternity to Eternity, two Worlds are within one another.*

We will not write obscurely or in a way that cannot be understood, but demonstratively with good evidence. We perceive and know that every life originates out of *anguish*, as if in a venom or poison; this is a dying, and yet it is also the life itself, as is plainly perceived in men and all creatures.

2. For without anguish or poison, there is no life, as is very well seen in all creatures—especially in man, who exists in three principles.

3. First: one principle is in the fire, where the "Great Life" stands, to which a dying poison—namely, the *gall*—belongs. This poison creates the "anguish-chamber" in which the fire-life originally arises.

4. Second: out of the fire-life, the second principle arises—namely, the light-life. Out of this, the noble mind with its senses or thoughts exists, in which we bear and understand our "noble image" <note>Boehme refers to the *Imago Dei*, the divine image or spiritual blueprint within humanity.</note>. For the fire-life in the heart originally arises from the death of the gall.

<margin>* The gall is the dying source or quality.</margin>

5. Third: we understand the third principle to be in the other "anguish-chamber"—namely, in the stomach or entrails. Into this, we stuff the four elements along with the constellation or *stars* <note>original: "Astrum"; in Boehme's cosmology, this refers to the celestial and planetary influences that govern the physical body.</note>. This is where the other anguish-chamber—the third center—is located: namely, the kingdom of this world, a house of stench and evil qualities. In this place, the third life—the starry and elementary life—is generated; it governs through the outward body by the reason of the third principle.

## Part II: Of Two Worlds within One Another. Chapter 4.

6. Now, we understand very well that in the heart—namely, in the center—there stands *another world* hidden. This world is incomprehensible to the starry and elementary "house" of qualities; for the heart sighs or pants after that other world.

7. And the spirit which is generated out of the death of the heart’s poison possesses that other world; for it is free from the poison which kindles the fire, and yet it dwells within the fire of the heart.

8. But **through its imagination,** the spirit conceives or comprehends the other world of the Liberty; it dwells in that Liberty, beyond the reach of the fire-source or property, but only so far as it brings or carries a longing pleasure toward or into God.

For if that were not the case, it could not possibly have entered into man; where there is nothing, nothing can come to be. But if something comes to be, it comes out of that which already exists. Every imagination models only its own likeness within itself and manifests itself in that similarity.

10. Seeing then that the substance of all substances is an eternal wonder in *three principles*, it therefore brings forth only wonders. 11. Therefore, we must now think upon these wonders and consider the kind and property of the *Eternal Mother* <note>original: "Genetrix"; Latin for "she who generates" or "mother." 13. And then, *secondly*, these *seven wonders* could not be manifested or revealed if the **ONE** only eternal will, which is called the Father, were not desiring.

# The Origin of Essence
### Form: From which the wonder of infinite and groundless multiplicity arises, and the

24. <margin>* Note.</margin>
§ 9. For this is just as if someone struck *steel and a stone* together. For they are two great hungers: that of the willing after substantiality, and that of substantiality after life.

§ 10. The will gives or provides **life**, and the substantiality gives or provides the manifestation or revelation of that **life**. Just as fire burns from a candle, so the will burns out of the essential substantiality.

# The Fifth Chapter.

## Concerning the Principle in itself: What it is.

->I.<-

We ought further to consider the first four Forms of Nature <note>In Boehme's system, the "Forms of Nature" are the seven properties that make up all reality. The first four (contraction, friction, anxiety, and fire) form the foundation of the material and dark worlds</note>; and so we shall find what a Principle is.

2. For it is properly called a Principle when a thing *becomes* what it *never* was before; where out of Nothing a source-quality <note>original: "source or quality"; this translates the German *Qual*, which Boehme uses to mean both a defining characteristic and a state of agonizing tension or "torment" that drives existence</note> comes to be; and out of that source-quality, a true life emerges with *understanding* and senses or thoughts.

3. And yet we know the true Principle to be in the *fire's* origin, in the fire-source or quality, which breaks through substantiality <note>Material or spiritual "body" or "essence"</note> and also through the darkness.

4. Thus we acknowledge and understand, first, the essence and property of the Fire as a Principle; for it creates and provides the origin of life and of all movement, as well as the strong power of fierce wrath.

5. *Secondly*: We understand and acknowledge that also as a Principle which: *First*, can dwell in the fire without being seized <note>original: "unapprehended"</note> by the fire; *Secondly*, which can take away the power of the fire; and *thirdly*, can change the fire's quality or source into a gentle love. *Fourthly*, that which is all-powerful over everything. *Fifthly*, that which has the understanding to break the root of the fire; and out of the fire *to create darkness*, and a dry hunger and thirst, without finding any ease or refreshment—just as the hellish quality or source is.

<margin>* Choked or made faint with thirst and hunger.</margin>

6. This is the *Abyss* wherein substance is \*ruined <note>original: "spoiled"</note>; where death rules with its sting, like a ruined or weakened poison.

7. In this state, there really is an essential life, but it *hates* and is at enmity with itself, where the true kindling of fire is not achieved; but it only appears as a *flash* without a steady flame.

8. And thus we give you to understand that in the *Eternal* there are no more than two Principles: namely <note>original: "viz": an abbreviation for the Latin *videlicet*</note>, one is the burning or blazing fire,

### II. Part. Of the Principle, what it is. Chapter 5.

20. 23. 24. 26. But the fire causes the substance, for it is a hunger, an earnest desiring; it must have substance or else it *extinguishes*.

27. *Understand this as follows.* Meekness gives, and the fire takes. *Meekness* is a going forth out of itself and gives a substance of its own likeness to every form from within itself.

28. And the fire devours that, yet it gives the Light out of itself. It gives that which is *more noble* than what it had devoured; it gives Spirit in exchange for substance.

### Chapter 5. Of the Principle, what it is. Part II.

30. Understand our meaning <note>original: "Minde"</note> correctly in this way: God the Father is, in himself, the **Liberty without or beyond** 
<margin>Regarding the Father's first and second Will</margin>
Nature; but he makes himself manifest in *Nature* through the Fire. This fiery Nature is his *property* <note>original: "property"; here meaning an essential characteristic or quality</note>.

31. Yet he is in himself the *Abyss* <note>original: "Abyss"; the bottomless, groundless void before or beyond creation</note>, in which there is no feeling of any source-quality <note>Boehme uses "source-quality" to translate the German "Qual," meaning both the origin of a thing and the "torment" or "anguish" of its existence</note> or pain.

32. Nevertheless, he brings his desiring will into a source-quality. In that source-quality, he creates for himself another or second will: a desire to go out of the source-quality and return to the Liberty *outside* or beyond that source-quality.

33. That same second will is his Son, whom he generates out of his own Eternal willing from all eternity.

34. He brings the Son forth through the fire, by breaking open the source-quality of Death—that is, through the earnest *severity* of his fierce wrath.

35. That very second will—the *Son* of God the Father—is what breaks or destroys Death (the stern, dark source-quality that *ignites* the fire). He goes forth through the Fire like a shining luster or gleam of the fire, and he fills or *satisfies* <note>original: "satiateth"</note> the first willing, which is called the Father.

36. For this gleam is as thin as a nothing, just like the will called the *Father*. Therefore, it can dwell in the Liberty—in the Father’s *Willing*. It makes the Father light, clear, bright, lovely, and friendly; for it is the Father's **Heart or Mercifulness.** <note>original: "Hertz oder Barmhertzigkeit" (German)</note>

<margin>Also with the Holy Spirit</margin>
37. It is the Father’s substance; it fills or satisfies the Father in all places, though indeed there is no specific place in him, nor any beginning or end.

38. Understand us further in this way: the Father’s fire *devours* the gentle substance—the water-source or quality of Eternal Life—into itself, into the fire's own essence, and thereby softens <note>original: "meekeneth"</note> itself with it.

39. In the fire, that substance must *as it were die*, for the fire devours it and *consumes* it.

<margin>* Note.</margin>
40. * And out of that consuming process, it gives forth a living, richly **Joyful Spirit**; and that is the *Holy Spirit*. He thus goes forth from the Father and the Son into the Great Wonder of the *holy substance* <note>original: "substantiality"</note>, and opens it perpetually and eternally.

<meta>This page continues Boehme's explanation of the Trinity through the analogy of fire, light, and air. He describes how the three persons of the Trinity function as a single, eternal "bond" of forces, and how life itself must emerge through a process of "anguish" or contraction, setting the stage for his discussion on the necessity of Christ's death.</meta>

<page-num>150</page-num>
<header>Part II. Of the Principle, what it is. Chapter 5.</header>

<margin>How the Trinity is but One God</margin>
41. Thus the Deity is an Eternal **Bond** <note>original: "Band"; refers to the connection or unification of the divine forces</note>, which cannot cease or pass away; and thus it generates itself from Eternity. The first is continually also the last, and the last is again the first.

42. And thus, understand the Father to be the fiery world; the Son to be the *Light-world* and Power-world; and the Holy Spirit to be the Life of the Deity—that is, to be the proceeding, driving Power—and yet **all is but ONE God.**

43. Just as the *Fire* and the *Light*, together with the *Air*, are but one single Substance; yet it divides itself into *Three* parts, and none can exist without the other. For the fire is not the Light, nor is it the wind <note>original: "wind"; referring to the air in motion or the breath</note> which goes forth out of the Fire.

44. Each has its office, and each has its own Substance within itself; and yet each is the other's life, and a cause of the other's life.

45. For the Wind blows the fire up, otherwise it would be *stifled* in its fierce wrath, so that it would fall into the dark death—just as stifling is the true, real *death* wherein the fire of Nature extinguishes and no longer draws substance into itself.

46. Of all this you have a good *analogy* <note>original: "similitude"</note> in the outward World and in all Creatures, showing how every Life—that is, the Essential Fire-life—draws substance to it, and that is its food to *eat*.

47. And the fire of its life consumes the substance and gives forth the *Spirit* of the power out of that which is consumed; and that is the life of the *Creature*.

<margin>
* shell.
How every life arises through Death
</margin>
48. And you see, quite rightly, how Life arises out of *Death*: it becomes no Life unless it breaks that <gloss>shell</gloss> out of which the Life should go forth. It must also go into the *Chamber of Anguish* <note>original: "Anguish Chamber"; in Boehme’s thought, "Anguish" (German: *Angst*) refers to the intense tension or contraction of the first properties of nature before they ignite into light</note>, into the Center, and must reach the fire-flash in the Anguish; otherwise, there is no kindling.

49. Although the Fire is manifold, and the Life is as well, yet out of the *greatest* Anguish also exists the greatest Life, as from a true Fire.

<margin>
* Purposed proposal.
+ Christ must suffer Death & we must die also
</margin>
50. Thus, dear children of God in Christ, we give you our knowledge and <gloss>intent</gloss> <note>original: "entent"</note> to ponder. We mentioned in the beginning that we would show you concerning the **Death of Christ.** *First*, why Christ had to die; *secondly*, why we must die also; and *thirdly*, how we rise again in Christ.

# II. Part. Of the Pilgrimage out of Death into Life. Ch. 8.

40. He has reason, therefore, to look for another and better life, since he must struggle here in *anguish* and misery. If he rightly understands how *well God intends* it for him, he will all the more seek and pursue Him, so that he might **not** build his hopes upon the earthly life.

41. Since he sees that this life is but *a valley of misery, affliction, and oppression*, and that he must spend his days here in hard *straits*, in misery, and in vain labor, weariness, and care, he should consider that God does not let these things happen in vain. Rather, God uses them to give him cause to seek the true rest, which is not found in this world.

42. Besides, he must expect death at any hour and leave his work to someone else. What is it, then, for a man to build his hope upon this world, where he is only a *guest*—a wanderer or pilgrim who must travel through the path or *passage* of his constellation? <note>original: "Constellation"; in the author's mystical theology, this refers to the external astral and planetary influences that govern a person's physical life and temperament.</note>

43. If he were to take up the ### Inward Constellation <note>The "inward constellation" refers to the spiritual state of the soul aligned with God, as opposed to the "outward" physical influences of the stars.</note>, oh, how happily and blessedly would he labor in God’s work, and let the *outward* world go, however it may be!

<margin>Note Well</margin>
44. A person in this world who intends to possess the Kingdom of God has *no better way*, nor can he have any better counsel or advice, than to continually consider and realize that he is in the *vineyard* of God in all his doings and possessions—whatever he is—and that he does it all for God.

45. His mind should look toward God in constant hope, trusting that he shall receive his wages for his labor from God, and that he labors in God’s wondrous works; therefore, he should be diligent in the labor he performs.

46. And when he must often serve a taskmaster <note>original: "driver"</note> or oppressor in weariness without pay, let him simply consider that he is laboring for God. Let him be patient in hope that God will surely grant him his reward in due time.

<margin>* Matthew 20:8</margin>
47. For * the Lord of the *vineyard* does not pay His laborers at noon, but *in* \* *the evening* when their day’s labor is finished—when we go home to our Lord, out of the valley of this <term>tabernacle</term> <note>A biblical term for a temporary dwelling; here, it refers to the physical body or the earthly life.</note>, and then everyone receives their wages.

<margin>

* Take note, you lazy and sluggish laborers.
</margin>

## The Third Citation:
### The Gate in the Center of Nature.

51. See, you locked-up knowledge <note>The author addresses the limited human intellect as "locked-up knowledge," which cannot understand spiritual truths without divine help.</note>: the ground or foundation of the world is like this; the origin of life is also like this. In this world, it cannot be any other way.

52. Unless a person is born again—**and then he is changed as the "new man"**—this oppression and driving force always clings to him in the *old man*. <margin>\* Note.</margin> \* This is the struggle of the Spirit against the flesh, where <margin>† Galatians 5:17.</margin> † *the flesh desires what is contrary to the Spirit, and the Spirit what is contrary to the flesh.* <note>The "Old Man" refers to the unregenerate human nature prone to sin, while the "New Man" is the spiritual nature transformed by God's grace.</note>

->*Question.*<-

53. Now Reason asks: Where does *this* have its origin?

<meta>This page continues the "Answer" started on the previous page regarding why God allows restlessness and suffering in the world. It begins to explain the first three "Forms of Nature"—the spiritual and physical forces that Jacob Boehme describes as the foundation of all existence.</meta>

->**Answer**<-

54. Answer: Behold! In the Center of Nature <note>The "Center of Nature" refers to the fundamental internal forces or "forms" that make up the material and spiritual world.</note>, there is *such* a thing, being, or substance; you only need to pay attention to it.

55. The eternal **will, which is called God, is free**; for it contains nothing but the light of majesty and dwells in the eternal Nothingness. Therefore, *nothing* can touch Him.

56. But His **desiring**, which creates the **Center** of Nature, has a specific property. Within it is a *harsh astringency* <note>original: "astringency"; a tightening, contracting, or densifying force that pulls inward.</note>—that is, the *first* property of nature. This force always attracts things to itself and receives even where there is nothing, where it has created a void; it takes it and *pulls* it all together.

57. Yet it cannot "eat" or consume it, nor is it profitable to it. Thus, it creates for itself anguish, pain, and restlessness, just as greed <note>original: "covetousness"</note> does in a human being.

58. The second form is its "drawing" or "sting." This is its servant or *child*, which pulls together whatever the desire wants. That is the "laborer" and represents the *inferior* man, who is evil, base, angry, and raging; he stings and throbs within the harsh astringency.

59. And the astringent harshness cannot *endure* this from the servant, but pulls it even more eagerly. Thus, the servant becomes more evil and base, more raging, and *assaults* the Lord’s house.

60. Consequently, the Lord tries to bind and hold the servant, and the servant tears away again with *malice*.

61. Then, seeing that the Lord—that is, the *harsh astringency*—cannot overpower the servant, they struggle together in great anguish, enmity, and opposition. They begin to form a "whirling-wheel" <note>Boehme uses the image of a whirling wheel to describe the intense, agonizing friction and motion of the lower forces of nature before they are transformed by light.</note>, harassing, murdering, and putting each other to death.

62. This is the *third form* of nature, from which arise wars, fighting, strife, the destruction of countries and cities, envy, and anxious, vexatious malice and wickedness. In this state, *one* always wishes the other dead; one wants to devour everything and draw it into oneself, wanting to possess it alone. Yet nothing gained is profitable; it is only *harmful*.

63. It behaves like the fierce wrath of nature, which swallows itself up, *consuming* and breaking itself; and yet, it also *generates* itself in this very way.

### 8. Ch. Of the Pilgrimage out of Death into Life. Part II.

<margin>* Note.</margin>
64. This is where all evil comes from; the devil, along with all evil things or substances, originates here. This is their source: it is how nature acts in the **Center**, you must understand, when it is without the Light. <note>The "Center" refers to the core properties of nature or the soul before they are enlightened by God's love and light.</note>

65. This is also how it is with the devil, who does not have the Light, as well as with evil men, beasts, herbs, grass, and everything that is hateful or hostile <note>original: "Enemicitious"; from the Latin *inimicitia*, meaning unfriendly or antagonistic.</note>.

66. For it is the "poison-wheel"—the source from which life originally arises—that whirls itself around in great anguish, stinging, raging, and breaking, until it *creates* another will within itself to escape the anguish. It then sinks itself down into death and **surrenders itself freely into Liberty.** <note>In this context, "Liberty" refers to the "Unground" or the peaceful "Nothingness" of God that exists before and beyond the turmoil of nature.</note>

67. In this way, it destroys the stinging and breaking through death and falls into the liberty of the first willing. This first will kindles the anguish of death with its quiet liberty; as a result, the anguish is *startled* <note>original: "terrified"; in the author's specialized vocabulary, this refers to a "shreak" or sudden transformative shock (German: *Schreck*) that turns darkness into light.</note>, death breaks apart, and out of the anguish comes a life of joy.

68. The same thing happens with a person when they are in anguish and enmity, when the sting of death and anger rages within them, making them anxious, greedy <note>original: "Covetous"</note>, envious, angry, and hostile.

69. Such a person should *not* continue in this evil condition, state, or behavior; otherwise, they remain **in the forms of death**, anger, fierce wrath, and *hellish* fire. If the "water-source" or cooling quality <note>The author uses "water" to represent the soothing, gentle element of God's spirit that tempers the "fire" of the soul's natural passions.</note> were *not* in them along with their flesh and blood, they would immediately become a *kindled devil* and nothing else.

70. Instead, he should examine himself and *create* another will within his evil anguish. He should move out from greedy malice into the liberty of God, where there is always plenty of rest.

71. He should *in death* sink down into patience and willingly surrender himself to the wheel of anguish. He must create a *thirst* for God's life-giving power <note>original: "quickening"</note>, which is the **Liberty**. In doing so, he sinks all the way through the anguish of death and falls into that liberty.

72. And so, when the anguish *tastes* the **Liberty**—realizing it is such a quiet, gentle quality—the anguish becomes startled. In that shock, the hostile, harsh death is broken; for this is a shock of great joy and the kindling of the life of God.

<margin>* A branch on the vine of Christ</margin>
73. This is how the * Pearl-branch or sprout is born <note>original: "Generated"</note>. It now stands in the trembling of joy, but it remains in great danger, for death and the quality of anguish *are still its root*.

80. Thus the Lily also goes into its Ether—that is, into the *free will*, into the light of the Majesty.

81. Understand it further in this way: when these two kingdoms divide themselves in the shock or transformation of Nature, then that shock is in itself a *flash*, and the cause of the Fire—that is, the kindling of Life.

25. For that which you now take for a friend has come out of the "chamber of anguish" <note>The internal state of the soul's dark nature before it is transformed by Light.</note>. It still contains the life of anguish; it has the source or quality of **Anger** and the Devil’s sickness, longing, or malady within it.

26. You must form or create a will in **God**. You must form or create a will out of your soul and, with that same will, *go out* from evil, wickedness, and malice into **God**. In this way, you will be introduced into God’s fire <note>The transformative light and warmth of divine love.</note>.

27. Understand: the "willing-spirit" <note>The intentional, active part of the human spirit that chooses to turn toward the Divine.</note> will kindle your soul. And *then*, reach after the life and spirit of Christ, and you will receive it. This will regenerate you with a new way of willing that will stay with you.

28. This is the blossom of your soul, in which the "New Child" <note>The regenerated spiritual self born from the union with Christ.</note> stands in the **image of God**. To that child, God gives Christ’s flesh and blood to *feed upon*.

29. And not to the "Adamical Ass" <note>The stubborn, unregenerate physical nature of man.</note>, as "Babel" <note>The author uses 'Babel' to refer to confused, worldly religious institutions and false dogmas.</note> strangely dreams—as if the wicked could participate in or become partakers of the body of Christ! Oh, no.

# The Tenth Chapter.

### *Concerning God’s Express-Reflex Image of Man: namely, the likeness between God and Man.*

->I.<-

1. We cannot see our substantiality <note>original: "substantiality"; the spiritual "matter" or essence that makes up the inner, divine body</note> or New Body in *this world* while we are in the earthly body. The Outward Man <note>The physical, fallen self.</note> does not know it; only the **Spirit**, which becomes generated and goes forth out of the New Man, knows its own Body.

2. But if we would gladly have knowledge of it, and would know whether we are in the New Birth, then we have no better proof or test for it than by looking at the likeness of God within us—which we understand to be our desires, our senses or *thoughts, and the mind.*

<margin>*Note.</margin>
3. These things contain within them the "Center of the spirit," out of which the strong will is generated and brought forth. In this will stands the right, true *similitude* <note>likeness</note> and the Image of God alongside flesh and blood—though the outward man does not know it.

4. For that very Image is not of this world, but belongs to another Principle—namely, the *Angelical world*. During this physical life, it remains within the Mystery or *Arcanum* <note>original: "Arcanum"; a secret or hidden inner essence.</note>.

5. It is like gold in a stone: the gold has a different *tincture* <note>original: "Tincture"; in alchemy, a transformative spiritual essence or quality.</note>, a different essence, and a different glow and luster; yet the coarseness or dross of the stone cannot comprehend it. The gold also does not comprehend the coarse dross of the stone, and yet that coarse dross—namely, the **Anguish** Center <note>A term in Boehme’s philosophy for the restless, "hungry" first principles of nature that provide the foundation for life.</note>—is a cause of the gold. The coarse dross is the mother, and the Sun—or *Sol* <note>original: "Sol"; the Latin word for Sun, often used in alchemy to represent the celestial father of gold.</note>—is the father.

6. In this same way, our "Old Adam" <note>The fallen human nature inherited from Adam.</note> and physical body are a cause of the New Body, for the old is the mother. Out of the old substantiality, the New Body originally arises; and God’s Spirit in Christ is the Father, just as the Sun is the father of gold. So also is God’s heart the Father of the New Man.

7. But now we cannot know the New Man any better *than* by looking at the "Center"—namely, in our desires, thoughts, and mind.

<summary>This chapter explains that the spiritual "New Man" is hidden within the physical body like gold in a stone, and can only be recognized through the transformation of one's thoughts and desires.</summary>

## 8. When we find ourselves in this state:
<margin>* Note: How we may know whether the Noble Lily-branch—namely, the Body of God’s Image—is being generated within us.</margin>
Namely, that our desire is directed entirely toward **God**; that our thoughts continually run in the will of **God**, and that the mind gives itself up completely in obedience *to* the will of **God**, and that the imagination or longing draws in <note>original: "lucketh," likely meaning "sucks in" or "feeds upon."</note> God’s power; then we may certainly know that the Noble Lily-branch <note>A symbolic term for the new spiritual life or the "New Man" born within the soul.</note> has been generated, that the Image of God exists in **substance**, and that God *has become Man* within that likeness.

9. At that point, it is necessary that the Noble Image be highly respected and cared for. The Old Adam <note>The fallen, sinful nature of humanity inherited from Adam.</note> with his lusts must be left no room or space, but must be continually put to death, so that the *New Man* may grow, become great, and be adorned with the wonders of Wisdom.

10. But now Reason asks: *What is this likeness then?*

11. *Behold!* **God** is Spirit; the mind, together with the thoughts and desire, is also spirit. The mind is the "wheel of Nature," the desire is the center—the first substance of Nature—and the thoughts are the essences <note>original: "Essences"; the fundamental qualities or "branches" of being.</note>.
<margin>* Or Branches.</margin>

12. For the senses or thoughts come out of these essences; they have their origin in the "sting of desire"—that is, out of the harsh astringency <note>A quality of contraction or tension within the soul's core.</note>. They are the bitterness, and they always run through the mind like an anguish wheel <note>The restless, rotating movement of the soul searching for peace before it finds God.</note>, seeking rest to see whether they may 
## attain the liberty of God.

13. These thoughts are what "strike up" the fire in the anguish wheel (the mind). In the moment of kindling—during the "crack" or terror <note>original: "Crack or Terrour"; the sudden, transformative flash where the soul's fire meets God's light.</note>—they *willingly* give themselves up to death. In this way, they sink down through the fire-source <note>original: "fire-source or quality"; the raw energetic drive of the soul.</note> and into "the Liberty"—into God’s arms. They go forth into that Liberty as a life born out of death.

14. They are the root of the new taste or relish which penetrates into God’s wisdom and wonders. They bring the desire out of the anguish of death; they fill their mother, the mind, and give it power from God’s own essence.

15. Thus, **the mind** is the wheel, or the true chamber of life—the soul’s own house, of which the mind itself is a part. This is true if the substantiality—the substantiality of the <term>Tincture</term> <note>original: "Tincture"; in this context, the spiritual life-force or divine essence that "colors" and transforms the soul.</note>—is credited to it: namely, the fire-life.
<margin>* Or dwelling of the soul.</margin>

16. For the mind exists out of the fire-life, and the fire-life dwells...

16. ...dwells in the Mind: but the Mind is *Nobler* than the Fire, for it is the movement of the fire's life: it creates the **understanding.**

17. The thoughts or senses are the mind's servants and are its most subtle messengers; they go into God and again out of God into necessity <note>original: "necessity"; in this context, it refers to the material realm or the world governed by physical needs and consequences rather than divine liberty.</note>.

18. And wherever they ignite themselves—whether in God or in necessity, namely in falsehood or wickedness—they bring that back home to the mind.

19. Therefore, the noble mind must often be *Lord* over evil or wickedness and stifle it in its anguish when the thoughts have entertained or loaded false or evil imaginations into the desire.

<margin>How God is all in all</margin>
20. Finally, understand it in this *manner*: *God himself is ALL and in ALL.*

21. But He goes out of the fierce wrath and finds the *light-and-power world* in Himself: He Himself creates them, so that the fierce wrath and all its forms are *only* a cause of life and a discovery of Himself in great wonders.

22. *He is the Ground <note>original: "Byss," meaning the foundation or ground of being.</note> and the Abyss; the* Liberty and also the Nature, in light and darkness.

23. And *Man* also is *all of this*, if he only seeks and finds himself *as God does.*

24. Our entire writing and teaching aims at this: how we must seek, create, and finally *find* ourselves; how we must generate or bring forth <note>The process of spiritual rebirth.</note> so that we may be ONE spirit with God; that God may be in US, and we in God; and that God's Spirit of Love in us may be the willing and the doing.

25. And it aims at how we may withdraw from the source or quality of anguish, so that we may introduce ourselves into the true *likeness* in the three worlds <note>Likely referring to the spiritual realms of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, or the Dark, Light, and Outer worlds.</note>, so that each of them may stand in their proper order, and that the *Light-world* within us may be LORD and hold the dominion.

26. In this way, the world of anguish may remain hidden within the light-world—as it also does in God—and so be *only* a cause of life and of God's wonders.

### Conclusion.

<margin>How humble is the likeness of God</margin>
29. Therefore, reader who loves God, know that a human being is the true likeness <note>original: "similitude"</note> of God, whom God loves deeply. God reveals himself in this likeness as in his own being; God is the center-point <note>original: "midlemost"</note> within man.

30. But he dwells only in himself; and if it happens that the spirit of man becomes ONE spirit with him, *then* he reveals himself within humanity—namely, in the mind, thoughts, and desires—so that the 

## Mind feels him.

31. Otherwise, in this world, he is far too subtle to be seen by us. Only the thoughts perceive him in the spirit—that is, in the willing-spirit <note>The "willing-spirit" refers to the faculty of human intent and desire directed toward the divine.</note>—for the will sends the thoughts into God, and God gives himself *into* the thoughts.

32. And *then* the thoughts bring the power of God to the will, and the will receives them with joy, but with * **trembling.** <margin>* or quaking</margin>

33. For the will acknowledges itself to be unworthy, seeing as it comes out of a rough lodging—namely, out of a wavering mind—and therefore it receives the power by *bowing down* <note>original: "sinking down"; a term for spiritual humility and surrender.</note> *before God.*

<margin>Power of Faith</margin>
34. Thus, out of its triumph, a soft, gentle meekness comes into being; that is God's true substance, and the will takes hold of <note>original: "apprehendeth"</note> that very substance.

35. And that conceived or grasped substance is, within the act of willing, the heavenly body; it is called true and right **faith**, which the will has received through the power of God. This faith sinks or immerses <note>original: "demergeth"</note> itself into the mind and dwells in the fire of the soul.

36. In this way, the image of God is complete or total, and God sees or finds himself in such a likeness.

37. And we should not think or conceive of God as a strange substance or a foreign thing; though to the wicked, indeed, he is a strange

41. But if he knew that God is so near him and yet he cannot grasp Him, that would be his greatest plague. 44. Even when he has spent a thousand years in the abyss, in the deep, he would still be *without* God in the darkness. And YET God is *in him*, but does not help him; also, he does not know Him. He only knows *of* Him and only feels His fierce wrath.

45. Understand it this way: just as a fire is in a stone, and the stone does not know it and does not feel it—except for the fierce, wrathful cause <margin>* Sun.</margin> * of the fire, which holds the harsh, astringent stone captive in a body—it feels *that*.

46. Thus, the Devil also feels only the cause of the light; that very cause is the fierce, wrathful center that holds him captive. He hates it and cannot endure it, and yet he has nothing else that *would* be better for him.

->**On the Sacrament**<-

The wicked do not partake of the Body of Christ; they receive the outward elements <note>original: "Elements"; the physical bread and wine used in the Rite of the Lord's Supper.</note>, but they do not discern <note>original: "distinguish"; meaning to spiritually recognize or perceive the presence of the divine.</note> the Lord’s Body. That Body is present everywhere in heaven and becomes food for the soul that reaches heaven. That same substantiality <note>original: "substantiality"; in the author's mystical theology, this refers to the spiritual "matter" or essence of the divine realm.</note>—even though it was indeed revealed as flesh and blood within Mary and took human nature into itself—**was at that very time (while Christ lay in the body or womb of Mary) in heaven** (John 3:13) within the "one Element" <note>The "one Element" refers to the pure, spiritual substance of the heavenly world, which the author contrasts with the four physical elements of our world.</note> in all places. It never traveled from some location many miles away to enter Mary. No; rather, the Word of the Deity unlocked the enclosed center which Adam had shut up in death under the anger of God. The Word introduced the divine substantiality into that virgin-like center which had been locked in death. (See page 80, etc.)

->**On Election and Reprobation**<-

If a person desires to be converted and enter into God’s light, they will be accepted. No decree of Election or Predestination <note>Election and Predestination refer to the theological debate over whether God chooses who will be saved before they are born.</note> is fixed against them. When someone loses the divine life and has nothing of God’s life within them, then all is finished and lost for them; they are and remain a devil. But God knows those who are His; He knows who will turn and be converted to Him. Upon those who turn falls the "Election" of which the Scripture speaks; and upon those who will not turn falls the "Reprobation," the hardening of the heart, or the withdrawing of light, etc. (See page 95, etc.)

All souls have proceeded out of one; they are, therefore, generated out of the perished or corrupted root. But since the new regenerated life in Christ has come again into a soul (or into one person), it is necessary that we cast our willing into the <term>regeneration</term> <note>original: "Regeneration"; the process of being spiritually reborn or made new through Christ.</note> of Christ. For in Christ, our souls have been generated in God again and have, in Christ, attained the divine image once more (page 208, verses 27–28).

The Kingdom of Heaven is within us; that is, we carry the divine substantiality, which is our heaven, within ourselves (page 153, verses 70–116). Christ became man in the heavenly virginity; the earthly <unclear>property</unclear> or quality merely clung to him (page 95, verse 72). The earthly part died away on the cross from its earthliness (page 83, verse 52). But we must all be born of that same virginity from which Christ was born; otherwise, we shall not see God (page 91, verse 67).

Neither the man nor the woman shall possess the Kingdom of God, but rather the virgin (page 100, verse 77). 

The Deity has longed to become flesh and blood; and although the pure, clear Deity remains Spirit, it has nevertheless become the <unclear>spirit</unclear> and life of flesh and works within the flesh. Thus, we may say that when we enter into God with our imagination and wholly surrender ourselves to him, we enter into God's flesh and blood and live in God; for the Word has become man, and God is the Word (page 5, verse 4).

"If the spirit of the soul <unclear>could</unclear> come into the eternal nothing, then he would come into that original ground from which eternal Nature and all creatures proceeded." — Jacob Boehme <note>original: "Behmen"; an English phonetic spelling of the author's name, Jacob Boehme.</note>

# The First Chapter.

## What Faith and Believing is.

<margin>* Matthew 6:33.</margin>

<margin>† Luke 11:13.

<margin>* Romans 8:26.</margin>

5. And so now, **Faith** is not a mere historical knowledge <note>original: "Historical knowledge"; the idea of knowing religious facts or dogmas without experiencing a personal, spiritual connection to them.</note> for a person to turn into articles of belief, depending only on them and forcing the mind into the works of reason. Instead, faith is one spirit with God, for the Holy Spirit moves within the spirit of faith.

<margin>* Or a spirit one with or in God.</margin>
6. True faith is the power of God, one spirit with God; it works in God and with God.

7. It is free and bound to no specific articles of belief, but only to the right and true **Love**. In this love, faith draws the breath of its life's power and strength. It does not lie in human will <note>original: "Arbitrium"; the Latin term for choice, judgment, or the faculty of the will.</note>, opinion, or conjecture.

8. For just as God is free from all inclination or deviation, doing what he wills and needing to give no account for it, so also is true faith free in the Spirit of God. It has no more than one inclination: namely, toward the love and mercy of God. This means it casts its own willing into God's willing and departs from the siderial <note>original: "Syderial"; referring to the stars or astral influences that Boehme believed shaped the earthly mind and personality.</note> and elementary reason <note>original: "Elementary Reason"; logic based purely on the physical world and the four elements.</note>.

9. It does not seek itself in the reason of the flesh, but in God’s love. And so, if it finds itself in this way, it finds itself in God and co-works—

<summary>This page defines true faith as a dynamic spiritual union with God and His love, rather than a mere intellectual acceptance of religious doctrine or "historical knowledge." 15. It is, in itself, the substance: it lives, and yet *does not seek* its own life, but seeks the life of the eternal, still *rest*: It goes out from its own life’s spirit and *possesses* itself.

18. 19. Just as the light is free from the fire, and yet is continually generated from the fire, and yet the source or *torment* <note>original: "source or Torment"; in Boehme’s thought, this refers to the restless, driving quality of nature (Qual) which can be painful until transformed by light.</note> cannot grasp or stir it: in like manner, I suggest to your understanding that faith is generated out of the spirit of life—namely, out of a continually burning fire. It *shines* in that same fire and fills the life's fire, and *yet is never grasped* by it.

20. But if it becomes grasped, then *faith itself* has entered into Reason as if into a prison; it is no longer in God, in *its freedom*, but has entered into the source-quality or *torment*.

21. It plagues itself, and yet *there* it may indeed be free; in the **Reason** it works **the wonders in the Fire of Nature,** and in the **freedom** it works **the wonders of God.**

# Chapter Two.

## On the Origin of Faith: and why Faith and Doubting dwell together.

->1.<-

<margin>Faith is God’s image: namely, the desiring, seeing, and mind.</margin>
Now, since faith is ONE spirit with God, we must consider its origin. For we may not say that it is a *figure* or *image* of Reason, *but it is God's image, God's likeness, an eternal figure.*

2. And yet it may destroy or corrupt itself during the time of the body <note>The "time of the body" refers to our earthly, mortal existence.</note>, or transform and alter itself into the source of anguish.

3. For in its own substance in the origin, it is merely a *willing* [an act of will], and that willing is a seed; and that seed must the fire-spirit—namely, the soul—sow into the freedom of God.

4. And so a tree grows out of that seed, upon which the soul feeds, and it calms or softens its fire-life: so that it becomes powerful, and gives its virtue <note>original: "virtue"; here meaning its inherent power or spiritual essence.</note> to the root of this tree. From this, the tree grows in the Spirit of God even into the wonders of the *majesty* of God, and blooms in the paradise of God.

5. And although it is so; we are thus, as it were, dumb or mute...

<summary>This page explains that faith is generated from the "fire" of life but remains free from its torment, serving as an eternal image of God that must be sown like a seed in divine freedom to grow.</summary>
<keywords>Jacob Boehme, Fire of Nature, Freedom of God, Soul as Fire-Spirit, Origin of Faith, Reason as Prison, Wonders of God</keywords>

...and may not be easily understood; for Reason insists on comprehending and seeing everything immediately. Yet we will set it out very clearly for all to see: why Faith and Doubting exist together—as if bound with a chain—so that there is a **vehement strife in Man** throughout the entire time he is a guest in <margin>* 2 Corinthians 5:1</margin> * *this tabernacle of earthly life* <note>original: "Tabernacle of the Earthly Life"; a biblical metaphor referring to the physical body as a temporary dwelling for the soul.</note>.

6. Unless he sinks down into himself so eagerly that he can bring the life's fire into the liberty of God; in that case, he is as if dead to the life of Reason, and though he lives, <margin>† Romans 6:10</margin> † *he lives to God*.

7. This is indeed a highly precious life for a person, and it is rarely or seldom found in anyone, for it is *like the first image which God created* <note>Boehme refers to the "first image" as the uncorrupted state of Adam before the Fall.</note>.

8. Although the mortal part clings to it, that part is effectively dead—as if a dead image hung upon him, a thing destined for corruption, in which the true person does not live.

9. For the true life stands converted; it exists in another world, in another principle, and lives in another source-quality <note>original: "source or Quality"; in Boehme’s terminology, a "source-quality" (Qual) refers to a fundamental state of being or a governing force of nature.</note>.

10. Therefore, understand us in *this way*: you see and know the origin of human life—how it exists in the mother's womb or body—and you see, moreover, how it operates and moves itself, namely, chiefly in four forms: fire, air, water, and earth (or flesh).

11. And although it clearly stands within these forms, it is in this regard nothing more than an animal life. For its *reason* comes to it from the constellations; it finds that the *sun* and the *stars* create a *tincture* <note>original: "Tincture"; in alchemy and Boehme’s philosophy, a "tincture" is a spiritualizing or transformative essence that gives qualities to matter.</note> in the four elements, from which reason and its operations—as well as pleasure and displeasure—originate.

12. But this is not yet the true human life by far, for this

### Reason seeks nothing higher, but only itself in its wonders.

13. Yet there is in man a desire and a great longing or panting after a higher, better, and *eternal life*, in which there is no such source-quality or torment.

14. And though it is clear that Reason does not apprehend or see it, yet a *mystery* lies within Reason, which tastes and knows it there; from this, the seeking originates.

15. By this we know that the same mystery was implanted during the first creation and belongs to man; we find that it consists in a desiring or longing—that is, in a magical seeking <note>original: "Magick seeking"; Boehme uses the term "magical" to describe the power of the soul's will or desire to draw spiritual reality into being.</note>.

16. Further, we find that with this *Mystery*, we are in a strange lodging within our "house" (the body). This same *Mystery* does *not* exist in the spirit of this world, for the world's spirit cannot grasp or find it. By this, we recognize the heavy fall of Adam <note>The "Fall of Adam" refers to the biblical loss of man's original divine state, which Boehme believes resulted in our spiritual blindness.</note>.

17. First, we find that Mystery in the will <note>original: "willing"</note> of the mind; it is a secret fountain-spring that opens itself in another principle <note>Boehme uses "principle" to describe a distinct realm of existence, such as the divine realm versus the material realm.</note>.

18. *Secondly*, we also understand that the Mystery stands hidden in the fire—in the source or quality of anguish—and opens itself through the anguish of the will.

19. And then *Thirdly*, we find how that same Mystery is held captive by the spirit of this world.

20. Just as the reason of the *outward* life has the power or ability to enter into that Mystery and destroy it, the Mystery does *not* come into the light because reason covers it. Therefore, the *Genetrix* <note>original: "Genetrix"; the creative or birthing power within the soul that "generates" spiritual reality.</note> cannot give birth, and so <margin>* Note.</margin> ### it remains as a hidden Mystery.

21. And so, when the body breaks [at death], the will has nothing *more* that can open the Mystery. Consequently, the fire—or the spirit of the soul—remains in darkness, and the Mystery stands eternally hidden within it, as if in another principle.

<margin>* Note.</margin>
22. Thus, we know that Mystery to be *God's Kingdom*, which stands hidden in the soul. It provides a longing pleasure and desire, so that the soul ### focuses its imagination in that Mystery.

23. Then the soul becomes magically "pregnant" in *that* Mystery, from which the will arises to go forth out of the fire-life <note>The "fire-life" represents the soul's raw, burning energy or ego before it is cooled and enlightened by God's love.</note> and into the Mystery of God.

24. And so now, if the soul lifts up its will and casts it into the Mystery, then the will becomes "impregnated" in the Mystery.

<margin>* Note.</margin>
25. For the will is longing, and it attains or becomes the "body" of the Mystery—that is, the substance of the Mystery, which is God’s substance. This substance is *incomprehensible* to human nature; in this way, the will draws God’s likeness or image onto itself.

26. So now, when the will is generated out of the soul's fire, its root still stands within the soul. Thus, there is no parting or tearing between the will and the soul; instead, the will becomes ONE spirit in *or with God* and becomes the soul’s garment, so that the soul—within the will—becomes *hidden* in God.

27. So, even though it dwells in the physical body, it is nevertheless surrounded and hidden in God by its *will*; and it exists in the will...

34. But he accepts a humble, lowly will that leaves the house of sins and desires sin no more, seeking its way out of *Reason* and into his love like an obedient, humble child; for that will is pure.

35. But as long as it stays stuck in opinion and guesswork, it is surrounded by opinion and is *not free*.

<margin>* John 6:37.</margin>

# The Third Chapter.

->*From where Good and Evil, Love and Anger, Life and Death, Joy and Sorrow Come: and how the Wonders of Nature appear in the Free Will of God; and yet how the Freedom of God does not mingle itself with the Wonders of Nature.*<-

---

->1.<-

And understand us further in *this way*: We perceive and have it sufficiently made known to us even in the *Holy Scripture*, as also in the light of Nature and in *all* and every thing or substance; that from the **Eternal Substance** all things proceed, both Good and Evil, Love and Anger, Life and Death, Joy and Sorrow.

2. Yet we cannot say that therefore Evil and Death come from God; for in God there is no evil, and also no death, and in eternity no evil enters into Him.
<margin>* Note.</margin>

3. The fierce wrath only proceeds out of the *fire* of Nature, where life stands as if in a *magic* <note>original: "Magia"; for Boehme, this refers to the creative, formative power of the will that brings spiritual ideas into physical manifestation.</note>, where one form desires and awakens the other. From this, the "Essences of Multiplicity" <note>original: "Essences of Multiplicity"; the diverse and varied forms of existence in the created world.</note> exist, and out of these, wonders are generated. In these wonders, Eternity manifests or reveals itself in **Similitudes** <note>original: "Similitudes"; reflections, images, or likenesses of the divine reality found within the physical world.</note>.

4. And yet we must say that in God's willing, there is a desiring, which causes that *magic* from which multiplicity exists.

5. And yet this multiplicity is not God's willing *itself*—which is free from all substance—but in the seeking or *longing* of the willing, Nature generates itself with all its forms. There, everything originally arises out of the Desiring—that is, out of the Eternal *Magic*.

## Chapter 3: Where Good and Evil Come From. Part III.

34. The matter is this: <margin>John 3:3, 5, 7</margin> *You must be born again through water and the Holy Spirit; otherwise, you will not see the Kingdom of God.*

35. This must be sincere and earnest. The will of our human reason must be broken; there must be a living movement of the will that breaks completely through reason and *strives* or fights against it.

36. Although this is not actually possible for the soul because it has become so perished or corrupted, there is no better counsel or remedy for it than this: it should make itself—along with all its reason and thoughts—as if it were **dead**. It must incline and unite itself solely and only with God’s **mercy** and surrender itself to it, so that no *other* space is left for reason, but rather reason must be compelled and subdued.

37. And if the will strikes down reason in this way, then reason is as if it were dead; and *yet* it still lives, but it becomes the servant of the true will—whereas before it wanted to be the lord.

38. For God's will must become the master over reason if reason is to perform or do anything virtuous that <term>subsists</term><note>To "subsist" here means to remain valid or to have a lasting, substantial existence in the eyes of God.</note> before God.

39. For nothing *remains* before God unless it is generated in God’s will.

41. Then the * wonders (or works) <margin>* Or works.</margin> that have been made or performed by or *with* the **spirit of reason** also remain before God. 43. In that state, only the outward principle of the work decays or corrupts—namely, its outward rule within the four elements.

44. And there, the *four* elements will be restored again into the *One*; there, all colors, forms, or varieties of the four will be *known*, along with EVERYTHING that has ever been generated within them.

Now, since everything that has been brought forth in nature is included and contained within God's willing <note>original: "willing"; Boehme uses this to refer to the divine intent or volition as a creative force</note>, we understand that nothing can enter into God’s willing unless it is *generated* or *made* within it. * Over or above.

### Part III. How a Person Should Live: Of the Future State of the Wicked. Chapter 4.

Mystery <note>original: "Mistery"; in Jacob Boehme’s theology, the "Mystery" (Mysterium) refers to the hidden, spiritual essence of reality or the divine foundation from which all things arise</note>; and it surrounds him and follows after him as a good work generated in God. 37. For when the body dies, then the Image <note>The "Image" refers to the spiritual, eternal form of a human being, created in the likeness of God</note> passes into the Mystery; that is, it becomes *manifest* in the Mystery of God.

38. For during the time of the earthly life, the outward principle was a *cover* before it, and that falls away with the dying of the body. Then the divine Mystery appears in the Image, and within it, all good deeds and works which had been generated in love through the will of God.

39. All the prayers and wishes of the honest and virtuous children of God stand in the Mystery. They incline themselves toward and unite themselves with the Image. 41. And all of this remains reserved for the judgment of God the Holy Spirit in the Mystery. There, *every person shall reap what he has sown here in his field*; there, it shall all spring up, grow, and blossom in a heavenly new Earth.

42. In that place, man will draw toward and put onto his divine Image the *body of the perfect Mystery of God*. He will see standing before him—that is, before the bodily or corporeal Image—his own righteousness, and see why he is so fair, beautiful, and bright.

43. He will *know* the cause of it and eternally rejoice in it, and he will compose or understand his song of praise or *Hallelujah* <note>original: "Hallelujah"; a Hebrew expression of praise meaning "Praise the Lord"</note> within that state, to God’s honor and His wondrous deeds.

This is gathered into the Anger <note>The "Anger" refers to the "wrath of God" or the dark, fire-principle that exists apart from God's light</note>, which will also follow after them. So they will ever continually *know* the cause of their source or quality <note>original: "source or quality"; likely translating the German *Qual*, meaning both "torment" and "quality/source-spring"</note> and torment; in that regard, they will be eternal enemies of God and of His children.
